name: Databricks
summary: A managed lakehouse platform built on Apache Spark and Delta Lake, with Unity Catalog for governance, on AWS, Azure or Google Cloud.
intro: Databricks runs Spark clusters, SQL warehouses, notebooks and jobs as a managed service, while the data stays in cloud object storage such as S3, Azure Data Lake Storage or Google Cloud Storage, as Delta Lake tables by default. Photon, a vectorised engine written in C++, replaces Spark’s JVM-based execution for SQL and DataFrame work without code changes, and is on by default in SQL warehouses and serverless compute.

Unity Catalog governs tables, files, ML models and other assets with one permission model and automatic lineage. Iceberg tables in Unity Catalog, including managed Iceberg tables (spec v1 to v3), are reachable by outside engines through its Iceberg REST catalog API for reads and writes. Iceberg tables owned by another catalog can be queried but are read-only in Databricks. Unity Catalog also exists as an open-source project under LF AI & Data, Apache 2.0 licensed.
strengths: One platform for ETL, SQL analytics, streaming and machine learning on open Delta and Iceberg files
Photon and serverless SQL warehouses make warehouse-style BI work on lake tables
Unity Catalog: fine-grained permissions and lineage across workspaces
Runs on all three major clouds
limits: Databricks bills in Databricks Units (DBUs), and on classic compute your cloud provider bills separately for the machines, so there are two bills to track
The formats are open, but much of the speed and convenience (Photon, predictive optimisation, serverless) is Databricks-only
Iceberg tables managed by other catalogs are read-only in Databricks
A large platform to administer: workspaces, compute policies, networking and permissions

story: By 2013, Apache Spark was taking off, but big data clusters were hard to set up and manage, and getting value from data meant gluing together a hodgepodge of tools. That year the team that started the Spark research project at UC Berkeley founded Databricks, with Ion Stoica as CEO. In June 2014 they unveiled Databricks Cloud: hosted Spark clusters with notebooks, dashboards and a job launcher, so a team could go from raw data to results without running infrastructure. It became generally available in June 2015, launching clusters on Amazon EC2.

Customers kept their data in cheap object stores like S3, but those stores had no transactions: a crashed update job left a table half-written, and queries over tens of thousands of objects were slow. In the service’s first years (2014–2016), around half of Databricks’ support escalations came from problems like these. The answer was Delta Lake, a transaction log on top of Parquet files, open-sourced in April 2019. In a 2021 CIDR paper, Armbrust, Ghodsi, Xin and Zaharia argued that this “Lakehouse” would replace the two-tier setup of a data lake plus a separate warehouse, which left warehouse data stale and copied twice.

Since then Databricks has added a C++ engine (Photon), governance (Unity Catalog, open-sourced in 2024) and AI tooling, and bought Tabular, the company of Apache Iceberg’s creators, to bridge the two main table formats.

choices.choice: Keep data in the customer’s own object storage
choices.why: Object stores let companies scale storage and compute separately: store a petabyte but run a cluster for a few hours. Databricks brought the compute to that data instead of loading it into its own storage.

choices.choice: A transaction log on top of Parquet files
choices.why: Object stores are key-value stores with expensive listing and weak consistency. Delta Lake records every change in a log, compacted into Parquet, which gives ACID commits, time travel and fast metadata lookups without a database server.

choices.choice: Open formats instead of a proprietary warehouse
choices.why: The lakehouse bet was that one copy of data in open files could serve BI, data science and ML. Tools like TensorFlow and PyTorch need to read large datasets directly, which is slow through a warehouse’s ODBC or JDBC interface.

choices.choice: Photon: a native C++ engine instead of the JVM
choices.why: Faster storage and data skipping had made queries CPU-bound, and tuning JVM-generated code hit limits, including garbage collection trouble on heaps over 64 GB. A vectorised C++ engine gave control over memory and SIMD.

timeline.text: Founded by the creators of Apache Spark
Databricks Cloud unveiled in June: hosted Spark with notebooks
Platform becomes generally available in June, on Amazon EC2
Lakehouse paper at CIDR argues for one platform on open formats
Acquires Tabular (Iceberg’s creators); open-sources Unity Catalog
Announces in July it is raising a strategic round at a $188 billion valuation
